BMI is a simple screening tool, not a diagnostic measure. Athletes with high muscle mass often have elevated BMI without excess body fat.

FAQ

What is a healthy BMI?▾
A BMI between 18.5 and 24.9 is considered healthy for most adults. However, BMI doesn't account for muscle mass or body composition — it's just one screening tool.
Is BMI accurate for athletes?▾
BMI is unreliable for athletes. Muscle weighs more than fat, so muscular individuals often fall in the 'overweight' BMI range despite excellent body composition. Use body fat percentage for a better measure.
What should I do if my BMI is high?▾
A high BMI may suggest excess body fat, but consult a healthcare professional for proper assessment. Combined with regular exercise and a balanced diet, gradual fat loss is the healthiest approach.

How BMI is calculated

Body Mass Index is your weight in kilograms divided by your height in metres squared (kg/m²). In imperial units the same number is 703 × weight in pounds ÷ height in inches squared. The calculator converts your units for you and rounds to one decimal place.

BMI categories for adults

BMICategory
Below 18.5Underweight
18.5 – 24.9Normal weight
25 – 29.9Overweight
30 and aboveObese

These are the standard adult cut-offs used by the World Health Organization. They are population-level screening ranges, not a diagnosis.

Why BMI can mislead if you lift

BMI only sees height and weight. It cannot tell muscle from fat, so muscular people often land in the "overweight" range despite a low body-fat percentage. It also ignores where weight is carried, age, sex and ethnicity. Waist measurements and body-fat estimates give a fuller picture, and a healthcare professional can interpret your numbers properly.

Who should not rely on BMI

  • People under 18 (growth charts are used instead)
  • Pregnant women
  • Bodybuilders and other very muscular athletes
  • Older adults, where muscle loss can hide excess body fat
